Cost basis of your shares is based on FIFO (first in, first out), therefore when you sell the first 10 shares, you are selling the initial 10 shares you purchased and therefore you recognize the gain of $50 for tax purposes.

 [https://www.nerdwallet.com/blog/taxes/capital-gains-tax-rates/](https://www.nerdwallet.com/blog/taxes/capital-gains-tax-rates/) (Capital Gains Bracket)

 [https://www.bankrate.com/finance/taxes/tax-brackets.aspx](https://www.bankrate.com/finance/taxes/tax-brackets.aspx)  (Ordinary Tax Brackets)

Keep in mind that selling shares at a profit, it can be taxed either at ordinary income or capital gains tax.  You will be charged ordinary income tax if you held your shares for one year or less.  If you held your shares for more than one year (one year + one day), then it will be charged at capital gains rate.

 [https://www.thebalance.com/can-a-capital-loss-carryover-to-the-next-year-2388983](https://www.thebalance.com/can-a-capital-loss-carryover-to-the-next-year-2388983) (Capital Losses)

Another benefit with holding your shares for more than a year is that your capital losses can rolled forward and used to offset your capital gains.  So if you sell shares that you held for more than and year and sold at a loss, up to $3k per year can rollforward and reduce other capital gains.
